Egypt Imposes Temporary Tariff on Imported Machinery, Local Firms Report Mixed Impact

CAIRO, June 21 – Egypt’s Ministry of Trade and Industry this week imposed a temporary 35% tariff on imported machinery products, a move officials say is intended to bolster domestic manufacturers amid concerns over a growing trade deficit. The measure, effective immediately and set for an initial period of six months, covers a broad range of machinery including industrial equipment, packaging machinery, and construction machinery.

The tariff has prompted a swift response from local machinery firms, who welcomed the protection from foreign competition but warned of short-term challenges as supply chains adjust.

“The government’s decision gives us a fighting chance to strengthen local production and invest in new technologies,” said Hossam El-Masry, CEO of NileTech Machinery, a Cairo-based firm. “We’ve already seen a rise in inquiries from domestic clients who previously imported specialized equipment.”

However, some manufacturers expressed concern that the higher cost of imported components—many of which are not produced locally—could offset the benefits. “While we support the intent behind the measure, our assembly operations rely on precision parts from Europe and Asia,” said Mona El-Attar, plant manager at DeltaMach Industries. “We are working with authorities to clarify which parts are affected and to seek exemptions where necessary.”

Industry analysts say the tariff could encourage investment in local manufacturing, but caution that firms may face disruptions as they adapt. “Several sites have temporarily scaled back operations while reviewing their sourcing strategies,” said Mahmoud Farouk, an independent sector analyst. “There’s uncertainty among workers about overtime and shift schedules, but most firms appear committed to maintaining employment levels in the short term.”

The Egyptian Union of Machinery Workers reported that no mass layoffs have occurred, but noted that some sites have reduced hours or shifted production to less import-dependent lines.

The Ministry of Trade and Industry said it would monitor the policy’s impact and consult with industry stakeholders before considering any extension.
